    AI Overview
    El Niño is heavily favored to emerge between May and July 2026, with a 61%-62% chance of development, likely strengthening by the fall and winter. Forecasters are monitoring a potential "Super El Niño" for late 2026, though spring uncertainty exists. This shift typically reduces Atlantic hurricane activity. 
    El Niño Forecast and Outlooks 
    • Formation Timing: A 62% chance of El Niño conditions is expected for the May–July 2026 period, with that likelihood increasing to over 80% by the fall.
    • Potential Intensity: Long-range models suggest a strong, or potentially a "Super El Niño" event, with Pacific Ocean surface temperatures possibly rising
      or more above average by late 2026.
    • "Spring Predictability Barrier": Forecasters warn that predictions made during spring (March–May) are less reliable, so confidence in the exact strength of the event will increase closer to summer.
    • Transition Phase: Currently, the climate is transitioning from a weak La Niña, with neutral conditions expected to persist into early summer before El Niño dominates. 
    Expected Global/Regional Impacts 
    • Hurricane Season: Early forecasts suggest a slightly below-average Atlantic hurricane season due to El Niño's influence, with 13 named storms and 6 hurricanes predicted. Conversely, it can enhance hurricane activity in the Pacific.
    • Global Weather: If a strong event develops, it can cause significant changes to winter storm tracks and global agriculture. 
    For the most current data, you can consult NOAA's Climate Prediction Center.

    Meteorologist at WISH-TV
    The latest European model seasonal forecast is calling for a potential Super El Niño to arrive by September. A Super El Niño is informally defined as when temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region in the tropical Pacific exceed 2°C above normal. El Niños historically have led to some of the warmest years on record, including 2024, and this will be no different. Combined with the ongoing trend of global warming, 2026 and 2027 will likely rank among the two warmest years ever recorded in Earth’s modern history. Super El Niños also supercharge extreme weather events around the world, including floods and droughts. In general, expect significant major climate impacts in the next 1.5 years globally. They also bring significantly increased odds of a below-average hurricane season in the Atlantic and a much above-normal season in the eastern Pacific. Stay tuned.

    🌀 NEW: The 2026 Hurricane Season forecast from Colorado State University is in. It calls for a below-average to near-average season in terms of the number of storms, hurricanes and major hurricanes due to a strengthening El Niño by the peak of hurricane season. Historically, strong El Niño events lead to greater wind shear and a suppression or lowering of tropical activity across the Caribbean, Gulf and Atlantic. While that would obviously be great news, remember, just takes one big storm to seem like an active year (which can still occur even during El Niño years like Betsy-1965, Camille-1969 and Michael-2018). Hope for the best, but always be prepared just in case. #Hurricane #HurricaneSeason #Florida
